name: Wendy Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including anything you keep private. What fills a normal day in your job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage five people who approve ingredient and allergy labels at a large ready-meal company. We compare the supplier sheet with the recipe and the print proof before a sleeve goes onto a meal. I've run the team for nine years and am good at the usual checks, but I need our food scientist for odd ingredients. I use AI every day to line up the two lists, then a person reads the original sheet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is good about it, and what matters at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like catching a changed ingredient before ten thousand sleeves are printed. Once I missed a supplier's sesame note because it sat under a new code; we stopped the batch just in time. I'm 43 with a bachelor's degree, a mortgage, and children aged nine and thirteen. My husband Dev drives a school bus on regular hours. My pay is ordinary for a manager, we have five months of expenses saved, and a few other food companies nearby have label teams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little automatic matching is already part of our day. If it stays a helper, our food scientist and my team still read the recipe and print proof. Dev's wage is steady and we have five months saved, so the mortgage feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to keep the supplier sheet beside every print proof. I'd tell Dev our jobs carry on much as before. I would not promise a computer can see an ingredient the supplier forgot to list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be comfortable. I have a job I know and a cushion for a bad month, though I would still think about the sesame note we nearly missed. I am not the cleverest food scientist here; that's why the team checks one another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this week I'd keep the existing AI comparison as a first pass and have the food scientist sign the five most unusual ingredient changes before printing. Through the first year of a plateau I'd stay with the current label team and add 150 monthly to emergency savings while our wages cover mortgage and the children's needs. I would not buy another tool to shave seconds off a safety check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our pay. I still get a little jolt when I read the word sesame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did that supplier note look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was a two-letter code in a margin instead of the ordinary ingredient line. The tool compared the main lists and missed it, and I almost did too. A small margin can hold a very big mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep a food scientist on the sign-off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because an unfamiliar ingredient can have another name on a supplier sheet. I know the routine labels; she knows which names point to the same allergen. The cost of one second pair of eyes is less than a recall.

I'd tell Dev a computer cannot see an **unlisted ingredient**.
think: My **job and mortgage** feel secure while AI stays a helper.
I still think about the **sesame note** my team nearly missed.
do: Keep the **existing AI comparison** as a first pass.
Get the food scientist's **sign-off** on five unusual changes before printing.
Save **150 monthly** while wages cover mortgage and children's needs.
feel: I feel **calm** about pay, with a jolt at allergy warnings.
S0.quote: The cost of one second pair of eyes is less than a recall.
fieldNote: Her **near miss** came from a coded supplier note outside the main AI comparison.
She relies on **human scientific sign-off** for unfamiliar ingredient names.
The family's **five-month cushion** and two wages support a calm baseline.

steps.text: Get food-scientist sign-off on five unusual ingredient changes before printing
Save 150 monthly only while wages cover mortgage and children’s needs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking recipes, writing label changes, planning print runs and answering retailers fill our office hours. A stronger system could do much of that and leave two checkers where there are five. The packing line still needs people, but I don't get to count its jobs as mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the director to test any new checker on awkward supplier codes before counting savings. I'd tell my team what errors it makes and ask for a staffing plan. I'd tell retailers there is still a named person to contact about a label concern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be retained because I know the team and use AI already, or I might be one of the three cut. My daily use of the current tool does not mean I can approve every new one safely. Dev's bus wage and our five-month cushion would protect the mortgage briefly, but I still need my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask for an eight-week paid trial of a new checker on old label changes, with the food scientist marking missed allergy codes if she agrees, and I'd learn its settings beside her if the director approves. If the trial works and the director approves rollout, I'd use the new AI to draft supplier-change summaries while people approve each printed sleeve. I'd set aside 200 monthly from my pay while both wages continue, and I would check posted label roles at two nearby food firms before leaving our current employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious for my own post, even as I want to run the trial. The cost of getting it wrong isn't just a staffing number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the system misses another sesame code?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop that part of the rollout and show the original supplier note to production. A beautiful draft cannot be eaten safely if the warning is missing. I'd rather explain a delay to the retailer than an allergy injury to a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check other firms if you could lead the pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pilot is work, not an offer to keep me. The other firms may be trying the same software, so I'd apply only when they post an actual opening. I can be curious and still keep a backup list.

Automate **supplier-change drafts** only after a successful trial and rollout approval, with human sleeve sign-off.
Save **200 monthly** while wages continue and check two posted local label jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If full AGI can read the supplier sheet, find the hidden ingredient and write the label by 2028, it can do the skilled parts of my desk. Dev still drives a bus by hand until robots around 2031, though its routing and booking could change earlier. A packing-line role might remain for a while, but I would need a real opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell staff the 2028 date and ask for written notice and paid roles. I'd tell Dev we should count his bus wage against all our bills, not simply hope it covers them. In public I'd say automatic labels still need a clear route for a parent to report a wrong warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my label role to end around 2028, and Dev's bus wage does not cover the mortgage, food and school costs together. Our five months saved is enough to look for work but not enough to replace my wage for long. I have woken up thinking of the children's lunch money while the office talks about speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the plant manager for a paid two-day batch-checking trial, with hygiene training, safety instruction and someone to cover my office shift; I'd complete it only if approved. I'd postpone the new car purchase before paying a deposit and keep that cash for the mortgage. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my desk job ends, I'd apply for a posted physical batch-checking role only if its pay with Dev's covers mortgage, food and school costs; if none opens, I'd use our reserve for a search among nearby firms while checking any support rules before counting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing my wage. Knowing AI tools early doesn't make five months of cash last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would batch checking survive until 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The physical work of opening and sampling meals might, while reports and schedules could go to AGI in 2028. Robots around 2031 could handle even the sampling. I'd need a wage for actual physical duties, not a quality title over a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son would be fifteen and our daughter eleven, so I'd tell them the old car can get us to school for now. I wouldn't ask them to solve a mortgage bill. I want to keep their ordinary week ordinary.

I'd tell Dev we must count his **bus wage against bills**.
think: I expect my **label wage to end** around 2028.
Dev's pay cannot cover **all family bills** without using our savings.
do: Complete a **paid batch-checking trial** only with approval, training and office cover.
Postpone the **new car deposit** and keep that cash for mortgage.
Apply after 2028 only for **posted physical batch work** whose combined wages cover essentials.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected wage loss despite five months saved.
S2.quote: Knowing AI tools early doesn't make five months of cash last forever.
fieldNote: Her **2028 label risk** precedes physical sampling robots around 2031.
The trial needs **hygiene training** and safety instruction plus shift cover and approval.
A plant move requires **an actual vacancy** and affordable combined wages, not a quality title.

steps.text: Complete paid two-day batch trial only with approval, hygiene training, safety and shift cover
Postpone new car purchase before paying its deposit
Apply for posted physical batch work only if combined pay covers mortgage, food and school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to find out whether I can do careful batch checks on the line. The label office faces AGI in 2031, and robots able to open and sample meals arrive around 2034. Reports from the batch line change with AGI too, so I won't call it a five-year safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to ask for paid plant practice before the desk work changes. I'd tell Dev we should try to save more while both wages come in. I would still ask for a parent to have a way to report a wrong allergy label.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might take a physical plant quality job if one is funded and open, but its pay might be lower than my manager wage. Five years could let us make a six-month cushion and reduce the car debt, provided Dev's hours hold. I still think the office title becomes a poor promise by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask for one paid supervised sampling day each month and complete it only if the plant approves hygiene training and Dev can cover school pickup. I'd put 150 monthly toward the car loan after mortgage, food and school costs, pausing if Dev loses hours. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for a posted physical sampling post only if its pay with Dev's covers those bills; otherwise I'd keep searching the other food firms while we have a reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but I can do something measurable in five years. I cannot make the plant offer a post by wishing for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on a sampling day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a meal from the line, match its lot number to the label and open it with a trained quality worker. I'd learn how to avoid contaminating the sample before claiming I could do the job. A desk certificate does not teach my hands a clean sample.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Dev really cover every pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if his bus route runs late. We'd ask a neighbour only if she agrees, or move the practice day; I wouldn't leave our daughter waiting at school. That has to be settled before I promise the plant a shift.

Pay 150 monthly on car loan only after bills while Dev’s hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'll be 53, our son twenty-three and our daughter nineteen. The mortgage might be smaller, but I will not spend a future raise today. Label checks still face AGI in 2036, and physical meal sampling faces robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should pay for actual line training while we still have work. I'd tell my team to learn why an allergy warning matters, not only where to click. I'd tell Dev we can plan the house and children's needs without betting on a machine company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have six months saved and a smaller mortgage if both our incomes hold; that's a possibility, not a number in the bank today. A physical quality role could keep me earning for a while if it is posted and paid enough, though its paperwork goes to AGI and robots reach the line later. I would rather know both label decisions and batch checks than depend on one title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask for a funded hygiene qualification and a paid line rotation; if approved I'd finish both with a trained worker. I'd keep five months of expenses in cash and pay 200 extra monthly on the mortgage only after food and school costs, stopping if Dev's hours fall. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd take a posted physical quality role only if combined confirmed wages cover household bills; otherwise I'd search the nearby firms with our reserve while robots remain about three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, not comfortable. A decade lets us build options, but the allergy label desk still has an end date in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest in AI shares instead of paying the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know which firm will win, and our mortgage interest is real now. I'd keep the cash reserve and reduce the loan before putting more into shares. A smaller house payment is a result I can count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the line rotation is not funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the label team and ask another food company about a paid training opening, without assuming it has one. I wouldn't spend the family reserve on a course with no shift. By 2036 the children will be grown, but we will still need a roof.

She separates **2036 label decisions** from physical line work facing robots around 2039.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My everyday checks could be cheap to automate before I have a paid line role, and Dev's bus driving can't cover all our bills by itself. Clear notice, a funded place learning physical batch checks and a posted wage that covers our mortgage would help. I also want a named person to answer when an automatic label check gets an ingredient wrong.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the parent who reads a meal sleeve for their child's allergy. They do not care whether our checker was human or software; they need the sesame line to be right. A clean label is a promise made at the dinner table.

headlineQuote: A clean label is a promise made at the dinner table.
portrait: Wendy, **43**, leads five ready-meal label checkers and uses AI daily to compare ingredient lists, followed by human review.
She has **nine years' experience** and a bachelor's degree, with ordinary skill, typical manager pay and five months saved.
She and Dev have **two school-age children** and a mortgage; his school-bus wage is steady, with some other local food firms.
Fast AGI threatens her **desk checks**, so she would test funded physical batch work while protecting family bills and allergy accuracy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her label wage before she qualifies for a paid line role.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice** and funded training tied to a posted physical batch-checking job.
A **named person** to answer for incorrect automatic allergy labels.
